title: Containers are processes: namespaces and cgroups
goal: By the end you can show that a container is an ordinary process on a shared kernel, build one by hand from namespaces, a cgroup and an overlay root, predict what happens when it hits pids.max or memory.max, and read the cgroup files the JVM reads to size itself.

warmup.q: A container started with `docker run --memory 1g --cpus 1.5` runs `java -jar ledger.jar` with no heap or GC flags, on a 12-CPU host with 8 GB of RAM. What does JDK 25 pick?
options: A 2 GB heap (25% of the host's 8 GB) and G1, because the JVM sees the whole host
A 256 MB heap (25% of the 1 GB limit), 2 CPUs, and the Serial collector
A 1 GB heap, 1 CPU, and G1
A 768 MB heap (75% of the limit), 12 CPUs, and the Parallel collector
warmup.why: The JVM reads the container's cgroup files at start-up: `memory.max` says 1 GB, so the default heap is 25% of it, and `cpu.max` says 150 ms per 100 ms, which it rounds up to 2 CPUs. With less than 1,792 MB, the machine isn't "server-class", so it picks Serial over G1. The lab box printed exactly that. The 2 GB answer is what a JVM does when it fails to detect the container, which is a real bug the last section covers.

sections.h: A container is a process on the host's kernel
sections.body:
Start a container that runs `sleep`, and inside it `ps` shows `sleep` as PID 1. From the host's side (the Docker VM, which runs every container on your Mac), the same process is PID 40037, its status file says `NSpid: 40037 1`, and `uname -r` prints `6.12.76-linuxkit` in both places. There is no second kernel and nothing booted. A container is a process.

The problem containers solve is old: run many services on one machine so that each acts as if it were alone. The ledger service shouldn't see the fraud service's processes, files or ports. A memory leak in one shouldn't get the other killed. A compromised one shouldn't be able to change the machine's clock or load a kernel module.

The simplest complete answer is a virtual machine per service: each gets its own kernel on emulated hardware. That isolates almost everything, and it costs a kernel, a boot and a reserved slice of memory for every service. Docker Desktop on your Mac does use one VM, the Docker VM this track has used all along, and every container runs inside that one.

Containers keep one kernel and use four things it already has. **Namespaces** give a process its own view of the system: its own PID numbers, hostname, network interfaces and mount table. A **cgroup** caps how much it can use: tasks, memory, CPU time. **Capabilities** and **seccomp** limit what it may ask the kernel to do. An **overlay** root filesystem gives it its own files on top of a shared, read-only image. Each one is an ordinary kernel feature you can use without Docker, and this lesson does.

The figure is the model for the whole lesson. One kernel serves everything, and a container is a few processes wrapped in those four layers. Lessons 1 to 11 still apply unchanged inside a container: the system calls, the scheduler, the page cache and the OOM killer are the same ones, because there is only one of each. That's also the price. A kernel bug that a container can reach is a bug in every container on the machine, which is why Docker's seccomp filter blocks dozens of system calls (lesson 1 of this track) and io_uring (lesson 11).

try.title: Find a container's process from the host
steps: Run this on your Mac, from the `labs` folder. It starts a container that sleeps, asks Docker for its process's PID on the host, and looks at that process from a second container that shares the host's PID namespace (`--pid=host`).
Predict the PID `ps` shows inside, and the `NSpid` line outside. The last line removes the container.

code.title: on your Mac, in the labs folder
code.src:
docker run -d --name sfz-os12-ledger --hostname ledger sfz-labbox:1 sleep 300 > /dev/null
docker exec sfz-os12-ledger ps -o pid,ppid,comm
pid=$(docker inspect -f '{{.State.Pid}}' sfz-os12-ledger); echo "host PID: $pid"
docker run --rm --pid=host --cap-add SYS_PTRACE sfz-labbox:1 bash -c "
  ps -o pid,ppid,comm -p $pid
  grep NSpid /proc/$pid/status
  readlink /proc/$pid/ns/pid /proc/$pid/ns/net /proc/$pid/ns/user /proc/1/ns/pid /proc/1/ns/net /proc/1/ns/user
  uname -r"
docker exec sfz-os12-ledger uname -r
docker rm -f sfz-os12-ledger > /dev/null

try.expect:
PIDs and namespace numbers differ on your machine:

```text
  PID  PPID COMMAND
    1     0 sleep
    7     0 ps
host PID: 40037
  PID  PPID COMMAND
40037 40008 sleep
NSpid:	40037	1
pid:[4026532698]
net:[4026532700]
user:[4026531837]
pid:[4026531836]
net:[4026531840]
user:[4026531837]
6.12.76-linuxkit
6.12.76-linuxkit
```

Inside, `sleep` is PID 1. The host knows it as 40037, a child of the container runtime's process, and `NSpid` lists both numbers, outermost first. Its PID and network namespaces have different numbers from the host's (`/proc/1` in a `--pid=host` container is the VM's own init). Its user namespace is the same one: Docker doesn't use user namespaces by default, so root in the container is root to the kernel. The kernel version is identical inside and out.

sections.h: Namespaces decide what a process can see
sections.body:
In the privileged lab box, `unshare --pid --fork --mount-proc --uts --net --ipc bash` starts a shell that can set its hostname to `ledger-box` while the box keeps `box-priv`. Inside, `ps -e` lists two processes with `bash` as PID 1, and `ip link` finds a loopback device that's down and no `eth0` at all.

The kernel keeps many tables that used to be global: the list of process IDs, the hostname, the network interfaces with their addresses, ports and routes, the list of mounted file systems. A **namespace** is a separate copy of one of those tables. Every process belongs to exactly one namespace of each kind, which `/proc/<pid>/ns/` shows as numbers such as `pid:[4026532834]`. A child starts in its parent's namespaces. `unshare`, or `clone` with flags such as `CLONE_NEWPID`, puts a process into new ones, and `setns` joins existing ones, which is how `docker exec` gets a shell into a running container. Linux has eight kinds:

| namespace | gives the process its own | in a container |
|---|---|---|
| pid | process numbers | the app is PID 1 |
| mnt | mount table | its own root file system |
| net | interfaces, IPs, ports, routes | its own `eth0` and `localhost` |
| uts | hostname | the container ID as hostname |
| ipc | System V IPC and POSIX message queues | no shared memory with neighbours |
| user | mapping of user and group IDs | root inside, nobody outside (off in Docker by default) |
| cgroup | view of the cgroup tree | its own cgroup looks like `/` |
| time | offsets for the monotonic and boot clocks | rarely used |

The PID namespace has two consequences you met in lesson 2 of this track. Its first process is PID 1 and takes on init's jobs: it must reap orphans, and the kernel delivers it only the signals it has a handler for, apart from `SIGKILL` sent from outside. And when that PID 1 exits, the kernel kills every other process in the namespace. Nested namespaces give a process one PID per level, which is the `NSpid` line.

Namespaces only change answers. A process in its own PID namespace sees 2 processes instead of 300, and it can still fork until the machine's task table is full, or allocate until the host runs out of RAM. Seeing less isn't the same as using less.

try.title: Make namespaces with unshare
steps: Creating namespaces needs the privileged box: from the `labs` folder, `docker compose -f env/labbox.yml run --rm box-priv`. (Docker's seccomp filter blocks `unshare` in the everyday box, as lesson 1 showed.)
The block prints the shell's hostname and namespace numbers, starts a shell in new PID, mount, UTS, network and IPC namespaces, and looks around. Predict which lines differ.

code.title: in the privileged lab box
code.src:
echo "outside: $(hostname), $(readlink /proc/self/ns/pid /proc/self/ns/uts /proc/self/ns/net | tr '\n' ' ')"
unshare --pid --fork --mount-proc --uts --net --ipc bash -c '
  hostname ledger-box
  echo "inside: $(hostname), $(readlink /proc/self/ns/pid /proc/self/ns/uts /proc/self/ns/net | tr "\n" " ")"
  ps -e
  ip -brief link show lo
  ip -brief link show eth0'
echo "outside again: $(hostname)"

try.expect:
Namespace numbers differ:

```text
outside: box-priv, pid:[4026532698] uts:[4026532696] net:[4026532700] 
inside: ledger-box, pid:[4026532834] uts:[4026532832] net:[4026532835] 
  PID TTY          TIME CMD
    1 ?        00:00:00 bash
    7 ?        00:00:00 ps
lo               DOWN           00:00:00:00:00:00 <LOOPBACK> 
outside again: box-priv
Device "eth0" does not exist.
```

Every namespace number changed, the hostname changed only inside, and the new PID namespace holds two processes, numbered from 1. `--mount-proc` mounted a fresh `/proc` for that namespace, which is why `ps` sees nothing else. The new network namespace has only a loopback device, down; `eth0` doesn't exist there (the error line comes out last because it goes to standard error). Back outside, the hostname is untouched.

sections.h: A cgroup decides how much it can use
sections.body:
The same kind of shell, moved into a cgroup with `pids.max` set to 20 and `memory.max` to 64M, stops twice. `forks.c` gets 19 children, and then `fork number 20 failed: EAGAIN`. `hog.c` holds 48 MB, and its next 16 MB gets it killed with exit code 137.

A **cgroup** (control group) is a set of processes that the kernel counts and limits together. You've used three of its controls in this track: `pids.max` in lesson 3, `cpu.max` in lesson 4 and `memory.max` in lesson 7. In cgroup v2, the default on current distributions and in the lab box, the groups form one tree of directories under `/sys/fs/cgroup`. Making a group is `mkdir`. Every process is in exactly one group, listed in that group's `cgroup.procs`, and writing a PID into that file moves the process. A group's limits apply to everything below it, so a limit on a parent group also caps every group under it.

Each kind of resource has a controller, and each controller has files:

| controller | limit | how much now | what happened |
|---|---|---|---|
| pids | `pids.max` | `pids.current` | `pids.events`: max |
| memory | `memory.max`, `memory.high` | `memory.current`, `memory.stat` | `memory.events`: max, oom, oom_kill |
| cpu | `cpu.max`, `cpu.weight` | `cpu.stat` | `cpu.stat`: nr_throttled |

Limits act where the resource is spent. A `fork` or `clone`, threads included, that would pass `pids.max` fails with `EAGAIN`. A page fault that would push `memory.current` past `memory.max` makes the kernel reclaim inside the group first, and if that fails, run the OOM killer on the group's biggest process. A group that has used its `cpu.max` budget is throttled until the next period. `docker run --pids-limit 20 --memory 64m --cpus 0.5` writes exactly these files, and so does the kubelet from a pod's limits.

One rule shows up when you build a group by hand. In cgroup v2, a group that hands controllers down to child groups, through `cgroup.subtree_control`, can't hold processes itself. The Try-it moves the box's processes into a child called `init` before it creates `ledger` for that reason. The stepper builds a whole container this way and runs it into both limits.

sections.h: Capabilities, seccomp and an overlay root finish the job
sections.body:
Root in the lab box can `chown` a file, but `date -s 2030-01-01` fails with `cannot set date: Operation not permitted`. Start the container with `--cap-drop CHOWN`, and `chown` fails the same way, still as root.

Without a user namespace, which Docker doesn't use by default, root in a container is user 0 to the kernel, the same user as root on the host. What stops it is that Linux doesn't check "is this user 0?" for privileged operations. It splits root's power into about 40 **capabilities**, each guarding a group of operations: `CAP_CHOWN` for changing file owners, `CAP_NET_BIND_SERVICE` for ports below 1024, `CAP_SYS_TIME` for setting the clock, `CAP_SYS_ADMIN` for mounts and much more. A process has a set of them, and the kernel checks the one the operation needs. Docker gives a container 14 and drops the rest, so the `CapEff` mask in `/proc/self/status` decodes to `cap_chown`, `cap_kill`, `cap_net_bind_service` and 11 others, and no `cap_sys_time`. `--privileged` gives all of them and turns seccomp off; that's the `box-priv` you've used for this lesson's experiments.

seccomp is the filter from lesson 1 of this track. It runs before every system call, and Docker's default profile refuses around 44 of them, including `mount`, `unshare` and the io_uring calls. Capabilities say which privileged operations a process may perform; seccomp removes whole system calls from reach, in case the kernel has a bug in one of them.

Last, the files. An image is a stack of read-only layers: `sfz-labbox:1` has 7. A container's root is an **overlay** mount: the image layers as `lowerdir`, plus an empty writable `upperdir` of its own. A read finds the file in the topmost layer that has it. The first write to a file from a lower layer copies the whole file up into the upper directory and changes the copy, which is copy-on-write again (lesson 7 of this track), per file instead of per page. A delete writes a marker, a "whiteout", that hides the lower file. `docker diff` lists the upper directory, and `docker rm` throws it away, so a container never changes its image. A hundred containers from one image share its layers on disk and in the page cache.

With `--cap-drop CHOWN`, the same root user can't `chown`. `docker diff` shows the upper layer: `C` for changed (`/etc/environment`, copied up and appended to, and its directory), `A` for added (`/tmp/settle.csv`) and `D` for deleted (`/etc/legal`, a whiteout). sections.h: The JVM reads the same cgroup files, and so should you
sections.body:
Under `--memory 1g --cpus 1.5`, JDK 25 chose a 256 MB heap, 2 CPUs and the Serial collector. In the same container with container support turned off, it chose a 1,984 MB heap and G1: sized for the Docker VM's 7.9 GB and 12 CPUs, in a container that gets killed at 1 GB.

At start-up, the JVM finds its cgroup in `/proc/self/cgroup` and reads its files. The default maximum heap is 25% of `memory.max` (`-XX:MaxRAMPercentage`). The CPU count is `cpu.max`'s quota divided by its period, rounded up (lesson 4 of this track) and capped by the CPUs in its cpuset. That number sizes the GC threads, the JIT compiler threads, the common `ForkJoinPool` and the virtual-thread carriers. The collector is G1 only on a "server-class machine", at least 2 CPUs and 1,792 MB; below that, Serial. A 256 MB container gets a 126 MB heap, about half, because HotSpot keeps a floor under small heaps. `java -XshowSettings:system -version` prints what the JVM detected, and `-Xlog:os+container=debug` prints how.

When detection fails, you get the 1,984 MB heap. That happened to real services: on Linux 6.12, the kernel stopped listing `cpuset` in `/proc/cgroups`, and JDK builds such as 17.0.12 and 21.0.5 treated that as a required controller gone missing. The bug report, JDK-8346874, shows the JVM logging "One or more required controllers disabled at kernel level" and sizing the heap from the host's memory, and an early JDK 25 build printing "System not containerized". JDK 25 has the fix (JDK-8347129); the lab box runs kernel 6.12, and its log says `Detected optional cpuset controller entry`. On JDK 17 or 21, run `-XshowSettings:system` in the real image on the real nodes, and look for `System not containerized`.

The same files answer production questions, which is the last tool for this track. Brendan Gregg's **USE method** checks every resource for utilization, saturation and errors. In a container, each has a file. CPU: `cpu.stat`'s `usage_usec` for utilization, `nr_throttled` and `cpu.pressure` for saturation. Memory: `memory.current` against `memory.max`, then `memory.pressure`, then `oom_kill` in `memory.events`. Tasks: `pids.current`, and `max` in `pids.events`. The `*.pressure` files are **PSI** (pressure stall information): the share of time tasks in the group waited for that resource, `some` when at least one waited and `full` when all did, as averages over 10, 60 and 300 seconds and a running total in microseconds. Two busy workers under `--cpus 0.5` stalled 6.2 s of 11. Inside a container, `/proc/pressure`, `free` and `/proc/meminfo` describe the whole VM, like `top`; the cgroup files describe your container.

refs.title: JDK-8346874: Linux kernel version 6.12 and newer breaks JVM container support
PSI: Pressure Stall Information (Linux kernel documentation)

analogy: A container is a tenant in a building, not a house of its own. Namespaces are the walls and the private mailbox: the tenant sees only their own rooms and their own post, and can paint the door number 1. The cgroup is the metered supply: so much water, so much power, and the breaker trips for this flat only. Capabilities and seccomp are the house rules at the front desk: you may hang pictures, you may not touch the boiler. The overlay is a furnished flat: the furniture comes with the building and stays when you leave, and anything you change is yours until you move out. The analogy breaks at the foundations. Real buildings have separate wiring per flat, but every container shares the one kernel, so a fault in the kernel is a fault under every tenant at once. That's the line where a VM, or a sandbox such as gVisor or Firecracker, starts to make sense.
in_your_world: Every pod you deploy is this lesson. The kubelet turns `limits.memory` into `memory.max` and `limits.cpu` into `cpu.max`, so a payment service's 137 with `OOMKilled` is lesson 7's OOM killer inside the pod's cgroup, and a p99 that jumps when a batch starts is lesson 4's throttling. Your Quarkus or Temporal worker JVM sizes its heap, GC and thread pools from those same files, which makes two checks worth doing once per base image: `java -XshowSettings:system -version` must show the container's limits, not the node's, and the heap should be set on purpose (`-XX:MaxRAMPercentage=60` to `75` is common for a JVM-only container) instead of left at 25%. When a pod is slow and its graphs look fine, read its PSI files: `cpu.pressure` and `memory.pressure` say how long it waited, which a utilization graph can't.
mistake: Treating a container as a small VM: assuming that root inside it is harmless, that `free` and `top` describe it, and that its kernel settings are its own. Root in a default Docker container is user 0 to the shared kernel, held back only by 14 capabilities and a seccomp filter, which is why `--privileged` or extra capabilities like `SYS_ADMIN` should be treated as handing over the host. `free`, `top`, `/proc/meminfo` and `/proc/pressure` describe the whole VM or node, so a container that looks idle in `top` may be throttled to death in `cpu.stat`. And `sysctl` settings like `vm.overcommit_memory` or `kernel.io_uring_disabled` belong to the node. Read limits and pressure from `/sys/fs/cgroup`, and decide privileges as if the container were a process on the host, because it is.

compare.note: A namespace changes the answers the kernel gives: which PIDs exist, what the hostname is, which interfaces there are. It never makes a call fail for using too much. A cgroup changes nothing a process can see, apart from its own cgroup files, and makes calls fail or processes die when they use too much: `fork` returns `EAGAIN`, a page fault ends in `SIGKILL`, a busy thread gets throttled. A container needs both: the left side alone can fork-bomb the host, and the right side alone sees and can signal every process on it.

steps.say: An image is just a directory. Copy a few programs into one, with the shared libraries `ldd` says they need. In the privileged box, on a scratch `tmpfs`:
steps.code:
mkdir -p /c && mount -t tmpfs -o size=200m tmpfs /c
mkdir -p /c/image/bin /c/image/proc /c/image/tmp
cp /tmp/forks /tmp/hog /c/image/bin/                     # built from os/c/l12/
for b in bash ls cat hostname ps; do cp $(command -v $b) /c/image/bin/; done
for lib in $(ldd /c/image/bin/* 2>/dev/null | grep -o '/[^ ]*\.so[^ ]*' | sort -u); do
  mkdir -p /c/image$(dirname $lib); cp $lib /c/image$lib

steps.say: Give it a writable layer. The overlay merges the read-only image with an empty upper directory; writes go up there.
Make the cgroup and set its limits. First move the box's own processes into a child group, because a group that enables controllers for its children can't hold processes.
steps.code:
cd /sys/fs/cgroup
mkdir init; for p in $(cat cgroup.procs); do echo $p > init/cgroup.procs 2>/dev/null; done
echo "+pids +memory +cpu" > cgroup.subtree_control
mkdir ledger
echo 20 > ledger/pids.max; echo 64M > ledger/memory.max; echo 0 > ledger/memory.swap.max

steps.say: Join the cgroup, then let `unshare` start a shell in new namespaces with the overlay as its root. `env -i` gives it an empty environment, as an image's entrypoint would get.
steps.code:
bash -c 'echo $$ > /sys/fs/cgroup/ledger/cgroup.procs
  exec env -i PATH=/bin LC_ALL=C unshare --pid --fork --mount --uts --net --ipc --cgroup \
    --root=/c/root --mount-proc bash -c "hostname ledger-box; ...; forks 500; hog 256"' &

lab.title: Model cgroups, PID namespaces and the JVM's view of them
steps: Read `Containers.kt`. `Cgroup` is a directory with limits and event counters, `PidNamespace` numbers its tasks from 1, `Task` holds one PID per namespace level, and `Host` is the one kernel. Making tasks, moving them, `forkIntoNewPidNamespace` and `kill` (with the PID 1 rule) are written for you.
Run the tests from the `labs` folder. All nine fail.

Write `checkPids`: walk `cg.lineage()`, and the first group that one more task would take past `pidsMax` counts `pidsEventsMax` and throws `SysError("EAGAIN", ...)`. `fork` and `startThread` already call it.

Write `touch`: charge the memory, then for each group in the lineage that is over `memoryMaxMb`, count `max` and `oom`, and kill the biggest task in that group's subtree until it fits, counting `oom_kill`.
Write `JvmView.availableProcessors` and `defaultGc`. The tests compare all of it with the files and JVM settings captured in the privileged box.
hints: `c.pidsCurrent + 1 > max` is the check: the new task is the one that would pass the limit.
Pick the victim with `c.allTasks().maxWith(compareBy<Task> { it.rssMb }.thenBy { it.hostPid })`, so ties go to the newest task, and call `kill(victim, ...)`, which also zeroes its memory.
`"150000 100000".split(Regex("\\s+"))` gives quota and period; `Math.ceil(quota / period)` turns 1.5 into 2. "max" as the quota means no limit.
Server-class means `cpus >= 2 && memoryMb >= 1792`: 2 GB minus 256 MB of slack.

drill.title: A cgroup from memory
drill.prompt: As root on a Linux host with cgroup v2, where `/sys/fs/cgroup` is the real root of the tree, write the commands that create a group `settle` with at most 50 tasks, 256 MB of memory and no swap, and half a CPU, then start `java -jar settle.jar` inside it. Then write where you'd look to see whether it hit each limit.

answer.src:
cd /sys/fs/cgroup
# (in the privileged lab box, first move its processes into a child group, as the Try-it does)
echo "+pids +memory +cpu" > cgroup.subtree_control   # controllers for the children
mkdir settle
echo 50 > settle/pids.max
echo 256M > settle/memory.max
echo 0 > settle/memory.swap.max
echo "50000 100000" > settle/cpu.max              # 50 ms per 100 ms
bash -c 'echo $$ > /sys/fs/cgroup/settle/cgroup.procs; exec java -jar settle.jar'

# did it hit them?
cat settle/pids.events          # max N: forks or threads refused with EAGAIN
cat settle/memory.events        # oom_kill N: processes the OOM killer took
grep throttled settle/cpu.stat  # nr_throttled: periods it ran out of budget
cat settle/cpu.pressure settle/memory.pressure   # how long tasks waited

recap: A container is ordinary processes on the one shared kernel: `NSpid` shows each one's PID inside and on the host, and `uname -r` is the same everywhere.
Namespaces (pid, mnt, net, uts, ipc, user, cgroup, time) give a process its own view. They change what it sees, never how much it can use.

A cgroup v2 is a directory under `/sys/fs/cgroup`: `pids.max` makes `fork` fail with `EAGAIN`, `memory.max` ends in reclaim then the OOM killer inside the group, `cpu.max` throttles. The `*.events` and `cpu.stat` files count each hit.
Root in a default Docker container is user 0 to the kernel, held back by 14 capabilities and a seccomp filter. `--privileged` removes both.
The root file system is an overlay: read-only image layers plus a per-container upper layer; the first write copies a file up.

The JVM sizes heap (25% of `memory.max`), CPUs (quota / period, rounded up) and GC (G1 only from 2 CPUs and 1,792 MB) from these files. Check with `-XshowSettings:system`, and read saturation from `cpu.stat` and the PSI `*.pressure` files.

quiz.q: From lesson 7: two containers run on one node. Container A, limited to 512 MB, leaks memory until it hits its limit; container B has no limit and holds 3 GB. Which process does the kernel kill?
options: B's biggest process, because it uses the most memory on the node
The biggest process in A's cgroup, because A's `memory.max` was hit and the OOM killer runs inside that group
Nothing: the kernel just refuses A's next `malloc`
Whichever process allocated last, in either container
quiz.why: Hitting `memory.max` starts reclaim and then the OOM killer for that cgroup only, choosing the biggest process inside it, and `memory.events` in A counts `oom_kill`. B is outside the group and never a candidate. `malloc` doesn't fail on Linux here, because the memory was promised long before; the failure happens at the page fault, as lesson 7 showed.

quiz.q: A container is started with its own PID namespace but no `--pids-limit`. Someone runs a fork bomb in it. What stops the fork bomb?
options: The PID namespace: it only has room for 32,768 PIDs
Nothing in the container: only a `pids.max` above it, or the host's own task limits, can stop it
The container's PID 1 reaps the children as they appear
seccomp blocks `fork` after the first thousand calls
quiz.why: A namespace renumbers processes; it doesn't count them against anything. Every child is still a task in the one kernel, so the bomb fills the host's task table until it hits `pids.max` of some cgroup above it or the kernel's global limits, and then every container suffers. That's what `--pids-limit` (and Kubernetes' pod PID limit) is for.

quiz.q: A pod runs JDK 25 with `limits.memory: 2Gi` and `limits.cpu: 500m`, and no JVM flags. What does the JVM choose?
options: A 512 MB heap, 1 CPU, Serial GC
A 1 GB heap, 1 CPU, G1
A 512 MB heap, the node's CPU count, G1
A 2 GB heap, 1 CPU, G1
quiz.why: `memory.max` is 2 GB and the default `MaxRAMPercentage` is 25%, so 512 MB. `cpu.max` is `50000 100000`, which the JVM rounds up to 1 CPU. With fewer than 2 CPUs the machine isn't server-class, so the default collector is Serial, whatever the memory. Using all 2 GB as heap would get the pod OOM-killed, since metaspace, thread stacks and native memory come on top.

quiz.q: Why does Docker's default profile block system calls like `mount`, `unshare` and the io_uring calls, even though the container's processes run as root?
options: Because root inside a container is a different, unprivileged user on the host
Because the calls would only affect the container itself
Because every container shares the host's kernel: without a user namespace, container root is user 0 to that kernel, and a bug in any reachable call is a bug for the whole host
Because those calls are too slow for containers
quiz.why: Docker doesn't use user namespaces by default; the Try-it showed the same user namespace inside and out. So the only things between a container's root and the kernel are its capability set and the seccomp filter. Removing whole system calls shrinks the kernel code a container can reach, which matters because that code is shared by everything on the machine.

quiz.q: A container edits `/etc/app.conf`, which came from its image. The container is removed and a new one starts from the same image. What does the new container find in `/etc/app.conf`?
options: The edited version: the edit was written into the image
The original version: the edit went to a copy in the old container's upper layer, which was deleted with it
Nothing: the file was moved to the old container's layer
The edited version, if the old container stopped cleanly
quiz.why: Image layers are read-only. The first write copied the file up into the container's own upper directory and changed the copy there; `docker diff` would have shown `C /etc/app.conf`. `docker rm` deletes the upper directory, and the image underneath never changed. Data that must outlive a container goes on a volume.

flashcards.front: Namespace or cgroup: which one limits how much memory a container uses?
flashcards.back: The cgroup (`memory.max`). A namespace only changes what a process can see.
The process is PID 40037 in the host's PID namespace and PID 1 in its own, nested one.

flashcards.front: What happens when a `fork` would pass `pids.max`?
flashcards.back: It fails with `EAGAIN`, and `pids.events` counts `max`. Threads count too.
It gives the container every capability (`CapEff` 000001ffffffffff) and switches its seccomp filter off.

flashcards.front: What happens on the first write to a file from an image layer?
flashcards.back: overlayfs copies the whole file up into the container's upper directory, then changes the copy.

flashcards.front: How does the JVM turn `cpu.max = 150000 100000` into a CPU count?
flashcards.back: Quota / period = 1.5, rounded up to 2, capped by the cpuset's CPUs.

flashcards.front: What do `some` and `full` mean in a PSI `*.pressure` file?
flashcards.back: The share of time at least one task (`some`) or all tasks (`full`) in the group waited for that resource.

terms.plain: One or more ordinary processes on the shared kernel, given their own namespaces, a cgroup, limited privileges and an overlay root.
A separate copy of one kernel table, such as PIDs, mounts, network or hostname, that a group of processes sees instead of the global one.
A directory under /sys/fs/cgroup holding processes that the kernel counts and limits together.
The part of cgroups that manages one resource, such as pids, memory or cpu, through its files.
One slice of root's power, such as CAP_CHOWN or CAP_SYS_TIME, that the kernel checks instead of user 0.
A mount that stacks read-only lower layers under a writable upper one, copying a file up on its first write.
Pressure stall information: how much of the time tasks waited for CPU, memory or I/O, per cgroup and for the machine.
Checking every resource for utilization, saturation and errors.

explain_back.prompt: A teammate says: "containers are lightweight VMs, so our settlement container can't affect the payment API container next to it." Explain what a container actually is, which parts of that claim hold, and which don't.
explain_back.answer: A container is a set of ordinary processes on the node's one kernel. Namespaces give them their own view: their own PIDs, hostname, network interfaces and mount table, so the settlement job can't see or signal the API's processes or bind its ports. A cgroup limits what they use, so if the job has a memory limit, a leak ends in the OOM killer inside the job's cgroup, and the API isn't a candidate. The overlay root gives the job its own files over a shared read-only image. All of that holds. What doesn't hold is the VM part. There is no second kernel: both containers make system calls into the same one. Without user namespaces, root in the job is user 0 to that kernel, held back only by 14 capabilities and a seccomp filter, so a kernel bug reachable from one container affects both. Anything without a limit is shared too: a job with no `pids.max` can fill the node's task table, one with no memory limit can push the node into a global OOM, and CPU without `cpu.max` is shared by weight. And node-wide settings, like sysctls, the page cache and disk bandwidth, belong to everyone. So: set limits on every container, never run them privileged, and use a VM or sandbox if you need a security boundary.

deeper.body:
User namespaces close the biggest gap in a default container. With one, root inside maps to an unprivileged user ID outside, so even an escape lands as nobody. Podman's rootless mode and Docker's `userns-remap` setting use them, and Kubernetes has been adding user namespace support for pods. They're not the default yet in most clusters because some volumes and images assume real root.

Where one kernel is too little isolation, sandboxes put something between the container and the host kernel: gVisor answers system calls in a user-space kernel of its own, and Kata Containers and Firecracker run each pod or function in a small VM with its own kernel. Both trade start-up time and some performance for a smaller shared attack surface.

Two more memory files are worth knowing. `memory.high` is a soft limit: above it, the kernel throttles the group's allocations and reclaims hard, but never calls the OOM killer, which gives a service a slow warning instead of a sudden death. `memory.oom.group`, set to 1, makes the OOM killer take every process in the group together, which suits a container whose processes are useless without each other.

The USE method has a classic first minute on a whole host, from Brendan Gregg: `uptime`, `dmesg | tail`, `vmstat 1`, `mpstat -P ALL 1`, `pidstat 1`, `iostat -xz 1`, `free -m`, `sar -n DEV 1`, `sar -n TCP,ETCP 1` and `top`. Each tool in that list reads files this track has opened: `/proc/stat`, `/proc/meminfo`, the per-process `/proc/<pid>/` directories and the network counters. In a container, check whether the tool reads the cgroup's files or the host's before you trust what it says.
